passage: “Why is the goat in the yard?” asked Dolma's mother as she came in from the field. Dolma looked at her feet. “I did it because... the gate was open, and the goat looked hungry.” “Who left it open?” “I did,” said Dolma. Anirban, her neighbour's boy, popped his head over the wall. “She wanted to feed him our cabbage leaves.” Dolma's cheeks reddened. “That's true. I'm sorry. I thought it wouldn't matter.” Her mother waited a moment. “I hear that you wanted to help the goat. Next time, ask me first.” Dolma nodded and shut the gate.

qa.q: Who left the gate open?
qa.a: Dolma.

qa.q: What did Dolma mean by saying the goat looked hungry, and what else did she admit?
qa.a: It was a real reason, since she wanted to feed the goat, but it was mixed with an excuse until she admitted she left the gate open and thought it wouldn't matter.

qa.q: What did Dolma's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She waited, listened for the need behind the reason, and asked Dolma to ask her first next time.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt after telling on Dolma?
qa.a: He may have felt he was helping tell the truth, or a bit awkward for exposing her, since he added it over the wall.

grounding: A child explains I did it because, mixing real reasons and excuses, and the adult listens for the need behind it.

passage: “Ines, why did you take the last biscuit?” asked Olga's teacher at break in Lisbon. Ines said, “I did it because I was hungry.” Olga, standing next to her, added, “She skipped breakfast.” The teacher paused. “Was that the only reason?” Ines rubbed her ear. “And... I didn't want Mateo to get it.” The teacher nodded. “Thank you for telling me both. I understand being hungry. Next time, ask me for a snack.” Ines said, “Okay.” Olga touched her arm. Later the teacher brought Ines a piece of fruit and said quietly, “Come to me anytime.”

qa.q: Which city was the school in?
qa.a: Lisbon.

qa.q: What did Ines's two reasons show about what she was feeling?
qa.a: She was really hungry, and she also felt some rivalry about Mateo, so one reason was true and one was less comfortable to admit.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that made honesty easier?
qa.a: The teacher asked if that was the only reason, thanked Ines for both, understood the hunger and offered a snack next time.

qa.q: How might Olga have felt while standing next to Ines?
qa.a: Olga probably felt protective of a friend, since Olga added that Ines skipped breakfast, and perhaps nervous about what would happen.

grounding: A child explains I did it because, mixing real reasons and other motives, and the adult listens for the need behind the explanation without treating every reason as proof of intent.

passage: When Noor came back to the science lab ten minutes late, Tushar Sir was waiting at the door. “Where were you? You left without asking.” Noor started talking fast. “I did it because a small boy from Class 1 was crying by the stairs. He'd lost his mother at the gate, and nobody was helping. And also the experiment was the same as last week, so I wasn't really missing anything.” Tushar Sir listened. “The first reason is a good one. The second one is an excuse, and you know it.” Noor looked down, then nodded. “Next time, tell me first, and I'll send someone with you. Did he find his mother?” “The guard called her. She came.”

qa.q: Who called the small boy's mother?
qa.a: The guard called her.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she started talking fast?
qa.a: Noor felt nervous about being in trouble and eager to explain her good reason.

qa.q: How did Tushar Sir respond to Noor's two reasons?
qa.a: He accepted the first as a good reason, named the second as an excuse and asked her to tell him first next time.

qa.q: How did Tushar Sir show he cared about the small boy?
qa.a: He asked whether the boy had found his mother, showing he listened to the need behind Noor's action.

grounding: Shows a child explaining her motives with a real reason and an excuse mixed together, and an adult listening for the need behind them.

passage: I'm Jahnavi, and I was there when Hemant explained the neighbour's broken flowerpot to Amma. It came out in a flood. “I did it because the ball was too bouncy. And the sun was in my eyes. And Kunal said I couldn't hit a six, so I had to try.” Amma didn't say, “Excuses, excuses.” She waited. Then she asked, “Which one is the real reason?” Hemant went quiet. “Kunal. He said I'm too weak for the team.” Amma nodded. “So you wanted to show him. That's the real thing. The pot still needs a sorry.” I don't know how Hemant felt inside, but he went next door by himself.

qa.q: Whose flowerpot did Hemant break?
qa.a: Hemant broke the neighbour's flowerpot.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he went quiet?
qa.a: Hemant felt hurt and embarrassed that Kunal had called him too weak for the team.

qa.q: How did Amma find the need behind Hemant's explanation?
qa.a: She waited and asked which reason was the real one, which brought out his wish to prove Kunal wrong.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi describe the moment?
qa.a: Jahnavi saw the flood of excuses turn into the real reason and noticed Hemant went next door by himself.

grounding: Shows a child explaining his actions with a mix of excuses and a real reason, and an adult listening for the need behind them.

passage: Monday: Ujjwal came to tuition without his worksheet. “I forgot it.” Urmila Aunty wrote it down. Wednesday: No worksheet again. “Our dog chewed it.” Urmila Aunty didn't laugh or scold. She noticed he had squinted at the whiteboard all hour and copied from the boy beside him. Friday: No worksheet. She sat beside him, away from the others. “You've given me two reasons this week. I don't think either is the whole story. What's really hard?” Ujjwal picked at the table. “I can't read the questions on the board. They're blurry. And I didn't want anyone to know.” Urmila Aunty moved his seat to the front and called his parents about an eye test that evening.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say happened to the worksheet on Wednesday?
qa.a: Ujjwal said their dog chewed it.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling behind the excuses?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt embarrassed and worried because he couldn't read the blurry board and didn't want anyone to know.

qa.q: How did Urmila Aunty get to the real need?
qa.a: She noticed his squinting and copying, didn't scold the excuses, and asked privately what was really hard.

qa.q: What would change if Urmila Aunty had treated the excuses as proof of laziness?
qa.a: Ujjwal might have been punished while his blurry vision went unnoticed.

grounding: Shows a child's explanations mixing excuses with a hidden real reason, and an adult listening for the need rather than treating reasons as proof.

passage: Lokesh, you're asking why I'm not angry about your broken kite? Sit, I'll tell you something. When I was nine, I, Baljeet, the great troublemaker of our lane, sneaked out Bauji's new cycle and scraped it all along a wall. Bauji held up the scratched mudguard. I talked fast: "I did it because Harpal said I couldn't ride a big cycle. And because you never let me. And the wall moved." It all came out at once, some true, some nonsense. Bauji didn't laugh and didn't shout. He asked, "Which reason is the real one?" I went quiet, then admitted I wanted Harpal to stop calling me a baby. Bauji nodded. The next Sunday he taught me to ride that cycle properly, and I polished the mudguard myself.

qa.q: What did young Baljeet scrape along a wall?
qa.a: Bauji's new cycle.

qa.q: Why did young Baljeet give so many reasons at once?
qa.a: Baljeet felt scared and ashamed about the scratch and grabbed at any excuse; underneath was real hurt at being called a baby by Harpal.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Baljeet?
qa.a: Bauji calmly asked which reason was the real one, which let Baljeet name the true need and led to riding lessons instead of punishment.

qa.q: How might Bauji have felt holding up the scratched mudguard?
qa.a: Bauji was probably annoyed about the new cycle, but stayed calm and curious enough to look for the need behind the excuses.

grounding: It illustrates a child's 'I did it because...' mixing real reasons with excuses, and an adult listening for the need behind the explanation.
